extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students of natural philosophy, rhetoric, and methods of learning
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critique on the arts of intellect (invention, judgment, memory, and delivery) and the proper methods for inquiry, proof, retention, and transmission of knowledge. The text diagnoses deficiencies in contemporary logic, induction, memory arts, and rhetorical practice and prescribes principles to correct them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of rational knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Rational knowledges are the keys of all other arts; they not only direct but confirm and strengthen other arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rational knowledge is likened to the mind as the 'form of forms' and must be prioritized because it enables and enhances other skills (Aristotle quote: 'the hand is the instrument of instruments, and the mind is the form of forms').

rubrics_metrics.name: Four intellectual arts
rubrics_metrics.description: The intellectual arts should cover four functions: art of inquiry or invention; art of examination or judgment; art of custody or memory; and art of elocution or tradition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation of learning systems should check that each of these four capacities is addressed: discovering, judging, retaining, and delivering knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for an art of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention (discovery) of sciences is deficient; logic as practiced does not invent the axioms of sciences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proper art of invention must be developed (beyond syllogistic logic) because inventions of sciences are not produced by current logical methods; absence of such an art limits discovery (analogy: mariner's needle enabling discovery of West Indies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper induction vs. enumerative induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Concluding upon an enumeration of particulars without a contradictory instance is no conclusion but a conjecture; the logicians' form of induction is vicious and incompetent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inductions must account for possible contrary particulars; do not treat an uncontradicted list of examples as proof. The mind naturally performs a better induction by distilling and comparing particulars, and methods should formalize that process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of syllogistic deduction in natural subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Middle propositions cannot (in subjects of nature) always be deduced from first principles by syllogism—the subtlety of nature resists such chaining.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid over-reliance on syllogistic deduction when treating natural phenomena; prefer methods that accommodate the complexity and variability of natural facts, and use syllogism mainly where appropriate (e.g., moralities, law, or parts of natural philosophy used for exposition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Source of error: intellectual powers and method
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors in knowledge arise more from weaknesses in intellectual powers and poor methods of collecting/concluding upon senses than from the senses themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remedy errors by improving methods, instruments, comparison, and rules of collection and inference rather than distrusting sensation wholesale; instruments and comparative methods can extend the sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-part program for invention of sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: Invention of sciences should be digested into two parts: experientia literata and interpretatio naturæ (learned experience and interpretation of nature).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programs and curricula should separate gathering/ordering of empirical learned facts from the interpretive method used to derive principles from them; both are necessary and complementary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of rhetorical invention (invention of speech)
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention of speech or argument is not true invention of new knowledge but is remembrance/suggestion and application of what is already known; its end is readiness and present use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place rhetorical invention after judgment: it is aimed at retrieving and applying stored knowledge to current purposes (being premeditated and adapted), not producing new scientific axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation (store of commonplaces)
rubrics_metrics.description: To procure readiness there must be preparation consisting of diligence: a store of common-places or premeditated 'places' handled in variety for the subjects one will speak about.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical pre-speech preparation includes framing prefaces, rehearsing typical openings, and pre-handling common argumentative places (e.g., for presumptions, testimony, equity vs. letter of law). This mitigates weakness at the moment of delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggestion (topics) — general and particular
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggestion assigns certain marks or 'places' (topics) to excite the mind to recall collected knowledge; topics are general and particular, and particular topics for each subject are useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaching and systems of invention should include both broad topical frameworks and specific, domain-tailored 'places of inquiry' that guide questions to ask and aid discovery in particular sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topics as aids to directed inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: The same places that help produce what we already know will also help direct inquiry: a faculty of wise interrogating is half a knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train question-framing: having anticipations and a large set of topics makes searches more direct and compendious; use topics both to recall and to discover.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syllogistic judgment: structure and methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgment by syllogism is reduction of propositions to principles via a middle term; reductions can be direct (probation ostensive) or inverted (per incommodum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess arguments by checking agreed principles, the appropriateness and election of middle terms, and the form of reduction; ensure clarity of propositional parts and of words that compose them (see analytics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Two pedagogical methods for judgment: direction and caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctrine of judgment should be taught by way of direction (framing true forms of consequence) and by way of caution (discovering subtle sophisms and illations—elenches).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction should both construct valid consequence-forms and expose fallacies with their refutations so students can both compose and critique arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study of elenches and equivocation
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine of elenches (examining fallacies and their redargutions) should cover ambiguity/equivocation and common adjuncts of essences (major/minor/priority/identity/etc.) as cautions against confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include training to spot equivocation, ambiguous predicates, confused divisions (categories/predicaments) and to use these as safeguards in inquiry and definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize rhetorical seduction (impression over reason)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a seducement that works by strength of impression rather than subtle fallacy—overruling reason by imagination—more properly treated under rhetoric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary that vividness, emotional force, or rhetorical skill can override logical assessment; design critiques and pedagogy to separate persuasive force from soundness of reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against cognitive biases (affirmative bias and imposed uniformity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind tends to be more affected by affirmative/present examples than by negatives/absences; it also tends to feign uniformity and relations where none exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for these biases by seeking counterexamples, resisting overgeneralization, and not imposing artificial symmetries on natural phenomena (e.g., forcing perfect circular motion models).

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for individual custom and disposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Each person's nature and custom (the 'cave' analogy) imposes errors and absurd imaginations; these must be recalled to examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote reflexivity: inquiry methods should include checks for personal prejudice, habituated perspectives, and locally cultivated fictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define terms at outset
rubrics_metrics.description: Words impose false appearances; therefore in controversies and disputations it is almost necessary to set down at the beginning the definitions of our words and terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin arguments and writings with explicit definitions to prevent disputes that are merely about differing uses of words; treat definitions as foundational to avoid ending where one ought to have begun.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate assignment of kinds of proof to subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four kinds of demonstrations—by immediate consent of mind or sense, by induction, by syllogism, and by congruity—and each has proper subjects and others from which it should be excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design standards of proof that assign rigorous forms where needed and allow remiss proofs where suitable; mismatching proof types to subjects has hindered knowledge historically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Custody of knowledge: writing (characters) and order of entry
rubrics_metrics.description: Retention of knowledge depends on writing (characters and order of entry) and memory; the disposition and collocation in common-places is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess systems for recording ideas by both the clarity of notation/characters and the ordering/digest of common-places; current commonplace methods are criticized as pedantical and lacking vitality—improve them toward practical use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical memory arts over ostentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The existing art of memory is able to produce ostentation (names, verses, jests) but is barren for serious use; memory arts should be useful to business and occasions, not mere tricks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate memory techniques by applicability to real reasoning and work tasks, not by their display value. Avoid systems that are prodigious in show but poor in applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memory principles: prenotion and emblem
rubrics_metrics.description: Memory should be built on prenotion (narrowing the compass of search by congruity) and emblem (reducing intellectual conceits to sensible images).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction in memory should teach prenotion to guide retrieval and use emblematic images to strike memory; other complementary aids are desirable and not inferior to these.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organ of tradition: speech, writing, gestures, hieroglyphics
rubrics_metrics.description: Tradition (delivery) has organs: speech or writing, but other media (gestures, hieroglyphics, real characters) can express cogitations where languages differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the organ of expression appropriate to the audience and medium: words/letters are dominant, but gestures and ideographic signs can function where linguistic barriers exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of notes (similitude vs. ad placitum)
rubrics_metrics.description: Notes of cogitations are either with similitude/congruity to notions (hieroglyphics, gestures) or ad placitum—by contract/acceptation (words and conventional characters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing notation systems, choose between iconic signs that resemble the concept and arbitrary signs accepted by convention; be aware of tradeoffs in universality and expressiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study of grammar as philosophical and popular
rubrics_metrics.description: Grammar has a popular use (learning languages quickly) and a philosophical use (examining the power and nature of words as images of reason); this latter should be more fully treated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage both practical language pedagogy and a philosophical grammar that clarifies how words map to concepts; treat accidents of words (measure, sound, accent) especially for rhetoric and poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtues of ciphers
rubrics_metrics.description: Ciphers should be (1) not laborious to write and read, (2) impossible to decipher, and (3) in some cases, without suspicion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or designing ciphers, balance readability/effort against security and plausible deniability; advanced schemes (e.g., omnia per omnia) are theoretically possible but must suit the human hands that use them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method as rules for delivery and to avoid sterile controversy
rubrics_metrics.description: Method should be part of logic (judgment) because the doctrine of method contains the rules of judgment upon what is to be delivered; excessive controversy often halts inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institute clear methods for organizing and presenting knowledge so that controversy leads to inquiry rather than to mere contention; method should guide both composition and exposition to promote productive discourse.
